entries.proposition: The phase 3 primary endpoint was changed from the phase 2 endpoint to major motor drop seizures, after a post hoc phase 2 analysis showed a larger signal.
entries.snippet: However, an additional post hoc analysis of seizures that led to a fall or would have resulted in a fall (drop seizures) showed a larger signal for efficacy (placebo‐adjusted median change from baseline of −30.6%, 95% confidence interval [CI] = −82.18 to 14.44). Based on these data, a phase 3 study was designed, and the primary endpoint was changed to reduction in major motor drop (MMD) seizures.

entries.proposition: The phase 2 LGS subgroup drop-seizure signal was non-significant (p 0.116 and 0.128).
entries.snippet: Analysis of the phase 2 study's LGS subgroup showed a placebo‐adjusted median reduction in drop seizures over the maintenance (17.08%, p = .1160) and full treatment periods (14.81%, p = .1279).

entries.proposition: Phase 3 primary endpoint: percentage change in the 28-day frequency of major motor drop seizures.
entries.snippet: The primary endpoint was percentage change from baseline in frequency of MMD seizures per 28 days during the full 16‐week treatment period

entries.proposition: The hierarchical testing order placed responder rate and global impressions before the non-seizure symptom domains and quality of life.
entries.snippet: the primary and key secondary endpoints were hierarchically tested in the following order: the primary endpoint, responder rate, Care GI‐I, CGI‐I, CGI‐I Non‐seizure Symptoms, QI‐Disability, and CGI‐I Seizure Intensity and Duration.

entries.proposition: Pharmacodynamic biomarker: plasma 24HC measured at screening and at two later visits.
entries.snippet: Baseline and postdose plasma 24HC levels, a pharmacodynamic biomarker related to the mechanism of action of soticlestat, were measured at screening, Day 57 and Day 113

entries.proposition: Primary result: no difference, -1.17 percent with p 0.785 (full) and 2.43 percent with p 0.778 (maintenance).
entries.snippet: The difference for soticlestat versus placebo in placebo‐adjusted median change from baseline in MMD seizure frequency was −1.17% (95% CI = –13.02 to 9.99, p = .785) during the full treatment period and 2.43% (95% CI = –10.86 to 15.14, p = .778) during the maintenance period
entries.anchor: Results, Effect on MMD seizure frequency

entries.proposition: With the primary missed, secondary endpoints are restricted to numerical comparisons with nominal p-values.
entries.snippet: Given the prespecified hierarchical testing, the absence of statistical significance for the primary endpoint restricts interpretation of secondary endpoints to numerical comparisons

entries.proposition: The authors report a numerical disruptive-behaviour signal (nominal p 0.032) and a seizure intensity-and-duration signal (nominal p 0.029) among key secondaries.
entries.snippet: soticlestat showed a potential benefit over placebo.

entries.proposition: Plasma 24HC fell by about 80 percent on drug against about 3 percent on placebo.
entries.snippet: A decrease in plasma 24HC levels was observed for all soticlestat‐treated participants (by approximately 80% vs. 3% with placebo; Figure S4).

entries.proposition: Treatment-related adverse events were more frequent on drug (39.6 versus 20.6 percent) and discontinuations for adverse events more frequent (see Table 3).
entries.snippet: Participants with TEAEs leading to study treatment discontinuation | 5 (3.7) | 19 (14.2)

entries.proposition: The authors state the pharmacodynamic reduction shows sufficient dosing and that the study was well designed.
entries.snippet: Levels of 24HC were reduced with soticlestat compared with placebo by ~80%, demonstrating sufficient dosing of soticlestat for effective inhibition of the catabolism of cholesterol to 24HC.

entries.proposition: The authors consider and reject several explanations for the non-replication, including placebo response, compliance and endpoint definition.
entries.snippet: Several potential reasons for the lack of replication of the phase 2 findings in the present study were considered and rejected.

entries.proposition: The endpoint was refined to reduce variability, on the assumption that caregiver counts differ when no motor component is identifiable.
entries.snippet: The aim of this modification to the endpoint was to further reduce variability, based on the assumption that seizure counts by caregivers are more likely to differ when there is no clearly identifiable motor component.

entries.proposition: The age range widened from 2-17 years in phase 2 to 2-55 in phase 3; the authors say adult inclusion does not explain the result (subgroup data not shown).
entries.snippet: However, in SKYWAY soticlestat was not associated with significantly reduced MMD frequency in either the pediatric or adult subgroups (data not shown), and so the inclusion of adult patients cannot explain the present findings.

entries.proposition: The authors state seizure-frequency change as a one-size-fits-all outcome may fail to capture clinical benefit and that other validated outcomes are needed.
entries.snippet: Although "change in seizure frequency" is the gold standard endpoint accepted by regulatory agencies, further research would need to focus on validating other outcome measures that reflect patient and caregiver perspectives in addition.

entries.proposition: The authors conclude the mechanism is not a suitable strategy for LGS, from one trial.
entries.snippet: In conclusion, these data suggest that targeting the CH24H mechanism of action is not a suitable pharmacotherapeutic strategy for the treatment of LGS.

entries.proposition: Supplement: the planned sample size was about 117 participants per arm; 136 and 134 were randomised.
entries.snippet: a sample size of approximately 117 participants per treatment arm was estimated to provide ≥85% power
entries.anchor: Supplementary methods, Determination of sample size

entries.proposition: Supplement: the QI-Disability inventory is a parent-reported questionnaire with 32 items in six domains.
entries.snippet: The Quality of Life Inventory-Disability (QI-Disability) tool is a parent/caregiver-reported questionnaire that evaluates quality of life in children with intellectual disabilities.
